title: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
metaTitle: How to Spot a Lowball Mineral Rights Offer
metaDescription: A retired E&P engineer breaks down the real tells of a lowball mineral rights offer in Montana and how to compare offers on fair, equal terms.
heroLead: After years watching offers get built on the operator side, I can usually tell within a few minutes whether a number is fair or fishing for a quick signature.
intro: Not every low offer is dishonest, some tracts genuinely are worth less than an owner expects, and that's a fair thing to hear even if it's disappointing. But there's a real difference between a legitimately conservative offer and one built to take advantage of an owner who doesn't know what questions to ask.
This is what I've learned to watch for, on both sides of the table, specific to how these deals tend to get worked in Montana.

sections.heading: The Tells I Learned To Watch For
paragraphs: A number that arrives before anyone has asked for your deed, your decimal interest, or recent royalty statements is a guess, not an offer, no matter how confidently it's presented. Real offers get built from your actual documents. Pressure to sign within twenty-four or forty-eight hours, especially paired with vague language about the offer expiring or the buyer moving on to someone else, is a classic tactic meant to prevent you from getting a second opinion or reading the paperwork carefully.

I'd also watch for anyone who won't explain how they arrived at their number when you ask directly. A legitimate buyer can walk you through their reasoning, even in general terms; someone hoping you won't look closely usually can't or won't.

sections.heading: Comparing Offers Apples To Apples
paragraphs: The only fair way to compare two offers is to make sure they're valuing the same thing: the same decimal interest, the same understanding of whether the tract is producing, and clarity on whether the number is for all your minerals or only a portion. I've seen owners compare a per-acre figure from one buyer against a lump-sum figure from another without realizing they weren't measuring the same quantity at all.

If a buyer's number seems unusually high compared to everyone else, that's worth scrutinizing too, since an inflated offer sometimes comes with unfavorable terms buried elsewhere in the purchase agreement, or simply doesn't survive to closing.

sections.heading: Pressure Tactics And Why They Work
paragraphs: Lowball tactics work because most owners sell a mineral interest once, maybe twice, in their lives, so there's no accumulated experience to draw on the way there would be selling a house or a car. Buyers who rely on that inexperience count on urgency and unfamiliarity doing the work that a fair number should. Family land, inherited interests especially, adds an emotional layer too, an eagerness to just be done with the paperwork and the phone calls that can make a quick, mediocre offer look more appealing than it should.
Slowing down costs you nothing. A legitimate offer will still be roughly the same, or the buyer will explain clearly why it changed, a week from now.

sections.heading: What A Fair Offer Actually Looks Like
paragraphs: A fair offer requests your documents before quoting a firm number, explains its reasoning when asked, gives you real time to review the purchase agreement, and doesn't penalize you for wanting a second opinion or an attorney's review. It should also account for the specific characteristics of your tract, its play position, whether it's producing, and its decline trajectory, rather than applying a flat, generic rate regardless of where in Montana your minerals actually sit.

If you get more than one offer and they're in a reasonably similar range once adjusted for the same decimal interest, that's usually a sign the market has priced your tract fairly, even if the number is smaller than you'd hoped.

faqs.question: Is a low offer always a scam?
faqs.answer: No. Some tracts are genuinely lower value, particularly non-producing minerals far from active drilling. The concern is offers built without reviewing your actual documents or delivered with heavy pressure to sign fast.

faqs.question: How many offers should I get before deciding?
faqs.answer: Two or three from buyers willing to review your actual decimal interest and documents gives you a reasonable sense of the market range without dragging the process out for months.

faqs.question: What if a buyer refuses to explain how they calculated their offer?
faqs.answer: That's a legitimate reason for caution. A buyer confident in their number should be able to explain the basic reasoning, even without disclosing every internal detail.

faqs.question: Should I be worried if an offer expires in 48 hours?
faqs.answer: Yes, treat that as a warning sign rather than normal business practice. Real offers built from real documents don't typically require that kind of rushed decision.

faqs.question: Can I negotiate a mineral rights offer, or is it take it or leave it?
faqs.answer: Most legitimate buyers expect some negotiation, particularly if you can point to specific comparable activity or documentation that supports a higher number.

faqs.question: What if a buyer's offer letter has no company name or contact information?
faqs.answer: Treat that as a serious red flag. A legitimate buyer stands behind their offer with a name, a phone number, and a way to verify who you're actually dealing with before any documents get signed.
